title: Talking to Claude
description: Write prompts that get great results on the first try.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Great Prompt
lessons.description: Context, goal, constraints, definition of done.

theory.title: Five ingredients
theory.body:
Claude is smart, but it can't read your mind. A strong prompt has **five parts**:

**Context**: where this happens and what is going on (`our Express API`, `the checkout page`).

**Specific goal**: one clear action and target (`add pagination to GET /users`).

**Constraints**: guardrails that start with words like `don't…`, `only…` or `keep…`.

**Definition of done**: how you will both know it worked (`done when npm test passes`).

**File references**: point at the files with `@path`, like `@src/cart/total.ts`.
theory.code:
Users report the cart total is wrong when a coupon is applied.   ← context
Fix the calculation in @src/cart/total.ts.                       ← goal + file
Don't change the public function signatures.                     ← constraint
Done when existing tests pass and you add a coupon test.         ← done

theory.title: A fill-in template
theory.body: When you're starting out, write the parts as labeled lines. Claude reads it fine, and you won't forget a part. (You'll learn more about `@` in the next lesson.)
theory.code:
Context: the login form in @src/auth/
Goal: show an error when the password is wrong
Constraint: don't change the API client
Done when: the error renders and tests pass

theory.title: Specific beats short
theory.body: "fix the bug" forces Claude to guess which bug. Every guess burns time and tokens (the small chunks of text Claude reads and you pay for). A concrete target like `GET /users under 200ms` beats a vague wish like "make it faster". Kip calls this "measure twice, prompt once".

exercises.prompt: You want Claude to fix a failing test.
options: The test 'applies coupon' in src/cart/total.test.ts fails since yesterday's refactor. Find the cause and fix the code, not the test. Done when npm test passes.
exercises.explanation: The better prompt names the test, the likely cause, a constraint, and a clear finish line.

exercises.prompt: Match each prompt fragment to the ingredient it provides.

pairs.left: "in the settings page of our React app"
"done when the toggle persists on reload"

exercises.explanation: Each fragment answers a different question Claude would otherwise have to guess: where, what, what not, and when to stop.

exercises.prompt: Which addition most improves the prompt "make the API faster"?
options: Naming the slow endpoint and a target, e.g. GET /users under 200ms
exercises.explanation: A concrete target and location turns a vague wish into a measurable task.

exercises.prompt: Why include a definition of done?
options: It tells Claude how to verify its work and when to stop
exercises.explanation: A clear finish line, like passing tests, lets Claude check its own work.

exercises.prompt: You want a new feature added to a component.
options: Add a 'copy link' button to the ShareMenu component in src/components/ShareMenu.tsx. Use the existing Button component and show a 'Copied!' toast for 2 seconds.
can you add some sharing stuff
exercises.explanation: Naming the component, the reusable pieces, and the exact behavior gets it right in one pass.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the missing ingredients of this prompt template.
exercises.code:
Context: the login form in src/auth/
___: show an error when the password is wrong
___: don't change the API client
Done ___: the error renders and tests pass
exercises.explanation: Labeling the goal, the constraint and a "done when" line makes sure no ingredient is forgotten.
exercises.hint: The template labels are Context, Goal, Constraint, and "Done when".

exercises.scenario: Your Express API's GET /users endpoint returns every user at once and is getting slow. You want page-based pagination added without breaking the existing mobile client.
exercises.sample: Our Express API's GET /users in @src/api/users.ts returns every user at once and is getting slow. Add page-based pagination: accept ?page and ?limit query params (default limit 20, max 100) and return { data, page, total }. Keep the response unchanged when no params are sent, so the mobile client doesn't break. Add tests in @src/api/users.test.ts; done when npm test passes.
exercises.explanation: Context, a precise goal, a compatibility constraint, a test-based finish line and @ file references leave Claude nothing to guess.

theory.title: @ means "look here"
theory.body:
Type `@` followed by a path to pull a file into the conversation, with **no space** between `@` and the path: `@src/utils/date.ts`. Press `Tab` while typing to **autocomplete** the path, so you don't have to remember it.

Add a trailing slash to point at a whole folder: `@src/components/`.

Referencing files saves Claude from searching and makes your intent unambiguous.
theory.code:
> explain @src/utils/date.ts
> What does each file in @src/hooks/ do?
> Refactor @src/api/client.ts to use the helpers in @src/lib/

theory.title: @ inside a full prompt
theory.body: File references are one of the five parts of a good prompt (context, goal, constraints, done, files). Combine them all:
theory.code:
In @src/lib/validators.ts, isValidEmail accepts "a@b".   ← context + file
Require a domain with a dot.                             ← goal
Don't change the function signature.                     ← constraint
Done when the new unit tests pass.                       ← done

exercises.prompt: How do you reference an entire directory?
exercises.explanation: @ is the reference prefix, and the trailing slash tells Claude you mean the whole folder.

exercises.prompt: You can't remember the exact path after typing @src/au. What helps?
exercises.explanation: Tab completes @ paths, so you never have to remember or mistype a long file name.

exercises.prompt: You want Claude to update the date formatting helper.
options: Update the date thing somewhere in utils so it shows the weekday
Update formatDate in @src/utils/date.ts so it includes the short weekday, e.g. 'Mon, 3 Mar'
exercises.explanation: An @ reference plus an example output leaves nothing to guess.

exercises.prompt: Match each reference to what Claude receives.
exercises.explanation: File paths pull in a file, while a trailing slash points at a folder.

exercises.prompt: Reference a file and a folder in one prompt.
exercises.code: Refactor ___src/api/client.ts to use the helpers in ___src/lib/
exercises.explanation: The @ prefix works for files and folders alike, so one prompt can point Claude at both.
exercises.hint: Both files and folders use the same prefix; a folder just ends with /.

exercises.prompt: Ask Claude to explain the file src/utils/date.ts by referencing it directly. Type the word explain, a space, then @ followed by the path.
exercises.hint: explain + @ + path, no space after @: explain @src/…
exercises.explanation: @path pulls that exact file into the conversation, so Claude doesn't have to hunt for it.

exercises.scenario: The signup form accepts invalid emails. Validation lives in a shared validators file, and the form component uses it. Ask Claude to fix it.
exercises.sample: In @src/lib/validators.ts, isValidEmail accepts strings like 'a@b' with no TLD, so the signup form lets bad emails through. Tighten it to require a domain with a dot, and update @src/components/SignupForm.tsx to show the error under the field. Don't change the function's signature. Add unit tests for valid and invalid cases; done when npm test passes.
exercises.explanation: Referencing both files with @, describing the bad input and naming a finish line makes the fix precise.

lessons.title: Show, Don't Describe
lessons.description: Paste errors, screenshots, and command output.

theory.title: Paste the real thing
theory.body:
Don't paraphrase an error. **Paste the full error text or stack trace** (the list of files and line numbers that led to the crash) straight into the prompt. Exact messages and line numbers are gold.

For UI bugs or mockups, **paste an image** with `Ctrl+V` or drag and drop a screenshot into the terminal.
theory.code:
> Build fails with:
  TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')
      at ProductList (src/components/ProductList.tsx:42:18)
  Expected the list to render empty. Fix the root cause.

theory.title: Bash mode with !
theory.body: Start a line with `!` to run a shell command yourself without leaving Claude. This is **bash mode**: the command runs directly and its output lands in the conversation, so Claude can see it. A space after `!` is optional.
theory.code:
> !git status
> ! npm test
> The test above fails. Fix the cause, not the test.

theory.title: A bug report Claude can act on
theory.body:
Follow this order: **reproduce** the bug → **copy** the full error → **paste** it → say what you **expected** → ask for the **root cause** fix.

For a visual bug, still use all five prompt parts: context (the screenshot plus what's wrong), goal, a constraint like `don't change the desktop layout`, a "done when", and `@` file references.

exercises.prompt: Your build crashes. What do you send?
options: The build has some type error about undefined, can you look?

Build fails with:
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')
    at ProductList (src/components/ProductList.tsx:42:18)
Fix the root cause.
exercises.explanation: The exact error and stack trace point Claude to the file and line immediately.

exercises.prompt: How do you paste a screenshot into Claude Code?
options: Ctrl+V (or drag and drop the image)
exercises.explanation: Claude Code accepts pasted or dragged-in images, which is great for UI bugs and mockups.

exercises.prompt: Match the input to the best way to share it.
exercises.explanation: Each kind of evidence has a fast, lossless way in, so Claude sees exactly what you see.

exercises.prompt: Why paste the exact error instead of summarizing it?
options: Exact messages include file paths, line numbers and details a summary loses
exercises.explanation: The precise text carries the clues Claude needs to locate the problem.

exercises.prompt: Order an efficient bug report to Claude.
steps: Copy the full error or stack trace
Add what you expected to happen
Ask Claude to find and fix the root cause
exercises.explanation: Real evidence plus expected behavior gives Claude everything to diagnose the issue.

exercises.prompt: You're inside Claude. Run git status directly using bash mode, so its output lands in the conversation.
exercises.explanation: The ! prefix runs the command yourself and adds its exact output to the conversation, so Claude sees real evidence.

exercises.scenario: Your header navigation overlaps the logo on mobile widths. You have a screenshot of the bug and know the header lives in one component file.
exercises.sample: [screenshot pasted] On screens under 400px the nav links in @src/components/Header.tsx overlap the logo, as shown. Fix the layout in @src/styles/header.css so the links collapse into the existing hamburger menu below 640px. Don't change the desktop layout. Done when nothing overlaps at 375px wide and desktop looks the same as before.
exercises.explanation: A screenshot, file references, a constraint and a visible finish line make a visual bug easy to fix.

lessons.title: Plan Before Code
lessons.description: Ask for a plan, review it, then build.

theory.title: Think first, type later
theory.body:
For anything bigger than a one-liner, ask Claude to **explore and plan before writing code**. Say it outright: `don't write any code yet`.

You review the plan, poke holes in it, and only then say go. Fixing a plan costs one message, while fixing a wrong implementation costs many. A typo fix doesn't need a plan; a migration does.

You can also nudge Claude to reason harder by asking it to **think** through tricky problems, e.g. `think through edge cases`.
theory.code:
> Read @src/billing/ and propose a plan for yearly plans.
> Don't write any code yet. List the files you'd change and why.

theory.title: The plan-first loop
theory.body: Five steps, always in this order. If the plan touches something you want left alone, say so at step 3; it's cheap to fix before code exists.
theory.code:
1. Explore:   "Read @src/billing/ …"
2. Plan:      "Propose a plan. Don't write any code yet."
3. Review:    "Revise it without touching @src/legacy/."
4. Implement: "Go ahead and implement the plan."
5. Verify:    "Run the tests and fix any failures."

theory.title: A planning prompt, five parts
theory.body: Planning prompts still need context, a goal, a constraint (`don't write code yet`), a definition of done (what the plan must cover) and `@` file references.
theory.code:
Our Next.js app has no roles yet. Read @src/lib/auth.ts and
propose a plan to add admin/editor/viewer roles.
Don't write code yet. Done when the plan lists files, steps
in order, and how we'll test it.

exercises.prompt: You need to migrate the app from REST calls to a GraphQL client.
options: Look through @src/api/ and propose a step-by-step plan to migrate to our GraphQL client. Don't write code yet; list files, risks, and the order of changes.
exercises.explanation: For a big change, a reviewed plan prevents expensive wrong turns.

exercises.prompt: When is asking for a plan LEAST necessary?
options: Fixing a typo in a README
exercises.explanation: Trivial, well-scoped changes don't need a planning round.

exercises.prompt: Claude's plan touches a file you want left alone. What now?
options: Tell Claude to revise the plan without touching that file
exercises.explanation: Correcting the plan is cheap, so fix it before any code exists.

exercises.prompt: Match the phrase to its purpose.
exercises.explanation: Each phrase moves Claude one step from exploring to building, so you stay in control of when code gets written.

exercises.prompt: Order the plan-first workflow.
steps: Ask Claude to read the relevant code
Ask for a plan and say don't write code yet
Tell Claude to implement the plan
exercises.explanation: Explore, plan, review, implement, verify: the order matters.

exercises.prompt: Complete the plan-first prompt.
exercises.code:
Read @src/billing/ and propose a ___ for yearly plans.
Don't write any ___ yet.
exercises.explanation: Asking for a plan and explicitly holding off on code keeps Claude exploring until you approve.
exercises.hint: Ask for a "plan" and hold off on writing "code".

exercises.scenario: You want to add role-based access control (admin, editor, viewer) to an existing Next.js app. You don't want any code written until you've approved an approach.
exercises.sample: Our Next.js app has no roles yet. Read @src/lib/auth.ts and @src/middleware.ts and propose a plan to add role-based access control with admin, editor and viewer roles. Don't write code yet. Done when the plan covers where roles are stored, how middleware checks them, which routes need protection (e.g. @src/app/admin/page.tsx), and how we'll test it.
exercises.explanation: Pointing Claude at the key files, forbidding code and defining what the plan must cover sets up a safe, large change.

mission.title: Prompt Smith
mission.intro: Forge a real prompt on a real codebase and see the difference specificity makes.
checklist: Pick a small real task and write a prompt with context, goal, constraints and a definition of done
Reference at least one file with @ (use Tab to autocomplete the path)
Paste a real error message or screenshot into the prompt
Ask Claude for a plan with "don't write code yet", correct it once, then let it implement
mission.explanation: Clear, grounded prompts plus a reviewed plan are the fastest path to correct code.

cheatsheet.description: The four ingredients of a strong task prompt.
Pull a file into the conversation; Tab autocompletes.
Paste an image; drag and drop also works.
Bash mode: run a shell command and add its output.
Exact stack traces beat paraphrased descriptions.
Ask for a plan first and review it before building.
Nudge Claude to reason more carefully on hard problems.
